subsubtopic: MEMBER'S SUPPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the present situation of ethnic minorities in the Soviet Union is worrisome. The Armenian, Lithuanian, Ukrainian, Jewish,

February 25, 1988
German, Moslem and other cultural communities continue to feel as though they are on the fringe of the Russian majority, which accounts for only 51 per cent of the Soviet people.
Yesterday's New York Times reported demonstrations and strikes in the independent region of Nagorno-Karabakh: most resident of that region-80 per cent-are of Armenian descent and are making official representations to Moscow with a view to being linked with Armenia.
Mr. Speaker, international press correspondents also report that Armenian representatives are to meet with Secretary General Gorbatchev to explain their situation and grievances, and hope they will be given a hearing.
At the same time, yesterday more than 100,000 people gathered in Erevan, the capital of the Soviet Republic of Armenia, seeking restitution to Armenia of that independent region which was annexed to Azerbaidjan during the 1920s under the Stalin administration.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to echo the claims of Armenian people in the Soviet Union. I praise them for their courage and tenacity, and I express the wish that a fair and equitable solution be found.

Mr. Speaker, on February 16, 1988, Soviet occupied Lithuania celebrated the seventieth anniversary of the restoration of its independence.
This peaceful religious celebration was attended by over
15,000	Lithuanians during the evening of the sixteenth. Unfortunately, we here in the West were unable to see the results of the celebration because the press had been shuffled out of the territory during the afternoon.
This peaceful, nationalistic celebration was interrupted by a Soviet militia of over 10,000 men, many of them coming from other parts of the Soviet Union. These men brutally beat the celebrants and hospitalized over 160 Lithuanians. Leaders and clergy of the Lithuanians were put under house arrest for three days with no contact with the outside world. There was even one instance in which a Lithuanian celebrant was beaten, had his head shaved, and was held prisoner for three days without food. Certainly this type of dehumanization is not just. Mr. Gorbachev's glasnost was not implemented in this situation. Why was a peaceful demonstration broken up with such brutality in a country that claims glasnost as its new policy?
I urge the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and the Government of Canada to pressure the Soviet Government and Mr. Gorbachev to live up to their policy of
glasnost and allow such peaceful demonstrations in the future. We all want peace, but not without freedom.

Mr. Speaker, once again Newfoundlanders are hearing that the federal and provincial Tory Governments are trying to close down the Newfoundland Railway.
One of the commitments when Newfoundland joined Confederation in 1949 was the maintenance of a rail link across the province. Until recently, Premier Peckford stood behind preserving that link. Today we have both the Premier and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) trying to cut a deal which will do away with this constitutional arrangement.
It is absolutely essential that, before any decision is made, Newfoundlanders must see the studies upon which any decision is to be taken. What will happen to the 650 employees and the communities whose livelihood depends on the railway? Before any decision is taken, a definite special economic development program for any communities adversely affected must be put in place. If one transportation system is to traded for another, there must be a perpetual commitment to the maintenance of that system.
It is time for both the federal and provincial Tories to be open and honest with Newfoundlanders and tell them what plans they have for the railway.

subtopic: CALL FOR LEGISLATION TO PROTECT UNBORN CHILDREN
CALL FOR LEGISLATION TO PROTECT UNBORN CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Advocates for Human Life, an association of lawyers across Canada, is pressing for legislation to provide protection for Canada's unborn children from abortion. They have added their weight to this crusade, as have the Knights of Columbus representing over 600,000 families, the Catholic Women's League of Canada with 128,000 members, Physicians for Life whose numbers are increasing daily, an increasing number of nurses, the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops plus all pro life groups, as well as hundreds of thousands of Canadian citizens.
Never in the history of Canada have we seen such a large number of Canadians working together to stop the killing of unborn human beings. Thursday, January 28, 1988, will go down in history as Black Thursday, a day on which the Supreme Court sentenced countless unborn babies to death by
February 25, 1988

abortion. This decision must be overturned. One does not solve social problems by creating innocent victims of a problem, our unborn children.
Therefore, I urge the Government to work in greater haste to enact legislation that will safeguard the life, liberty, and sanctity of every human person, including unborn children.

Mr. Speaker, under its five-year corporate plan, Canada Post has lowered its delivery standards, unable as it was to meet the previous ones. A postal services independant study has shown that one out of five letters is still not delivered on schedule, despite the lower standards. Mr. Speaker, Canadians deserve a better service.
As of today, the Minister and Canada Post Corporation have still not announced the measures they intend to take in order to ensure that the minimum standards they have already lowered will be met.
The climate in the Canada Post workplace is explosive. Why does the Minister encourage the confrontational style Canada Post adopted vis-a-vis its employees? How can the mail be delivered on time if those who move it are not motivated but rather frustrated?

subtopic: SOUTH KOREA-PLIGHT OF PRISONERS OF CONSCIENCE
SOUTH KOREA-PLIGHT OF PRISONERS OF CONSCIENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope I speak for all Members of Parliament in supporting Amnesty International's call on the new President of South Korea, inaugurated yesterday, to demonstrate his declared commitment to human rights by releasing all prisoners of conscience and by commuting all pending death sentences for so-called anti-state activities.
The continued detention of South Koreans for the peaceful exercise of their rights of freedom of expression and association belies the membership which South Korea would obviously like to claim as part of the democratic world. The fact is that South Korea's so-called economic miracle, often lauded by right-wing Canadians, has been bought at the price of much
political oppression. A rising GNP accompanied by rising rates of detention and suppression of dissent is not progress.
I call on the new president, Roh Tae-woo, to usher in a new era and declare the amnesty called for by Amnesty International.

maintopic: OBITUARY TRIBUTE TO QUEBEC FEDERATION OF LABOUR PERMANENT DELEGATES
OBITUARY TRIBUTE TO QUEBEC FEDERATION OF LABOUR PERMANENT DELEGATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with great sorrow and sadness that we learned last Tuesday that four high-ranking members of QFL Construction were killed while on duty.
They are: Guy Perreault, Director General, QFL Construction; Jean-Claude Sureau, Director, Association nationale des travailleurs en tuyauterie; Claude Proteau, Assistant Director General, Federation interprovinciale des ouvriers en electri-cite\ and Gaetan Boucher, union representative, Association nationale des mecaniciens industriels.
On behalf of my colleague, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux), and all the members of the Quebec Caucus, I would like to offer my deepest sympathies to all QFL members, who have lost valuable colleagues, and to the family and friends, so sorely tried.
I had the opportunity to work with some of these men, but I am well aware of the dedication of all of them to the cause of Canadian workers.
I would like also, on behalf of the Government, to offer our condolences to the friends and relatives of the pilot, Jean Verriere, and the copilot, Gary Gadouas.

Mr. Speaker, on November 7, 1986, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan), along with members of the Nova Scotia Government, announced a clean-up agreement for the Sydney tar ponds. The Minister said:
The tar ponds are an environmental menace to the health of the Sydney
residents.
Yet the Government continues to drag its collective feet on this very important project.
The Minister also said at that time that the workers of the coke ovens who would be losing their jobs would be offered

February 25, 1988
assistance by the federal Government in preparing for and obtaining new employment. Coke oven employees have already lost their jobs but nothing has been put in place.
Background information on that meeting of November 7 indicated that the federal Government said a CEIC industrial adjustment service agreement "may also be negotiated to assist those displaced workers presently employed at the Sysco coke ovens in preparing for and endeavouring to obtain alternate employment". Where is this assistance and where is this agreement? Why can the people of Sydney not rely on the promises of the Government?

Mr. Speaker, 70 years ago on February 24, 1918, Estonia became a free and independent nation. The Soviet Union brought an end to that freedom in 1940 when Estonia and other Baltic states were forcibly annexed to the U.S.S.R. Estonia remains occupied by Soviet troops to this day.
Canada's position on the illegal occupation of the Baltic nations is clearly stated in the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mul-roney) message to the Estonian community marking this seventieth anniversary of Estonian independence, and I quote:
Canada has never recognized in law this act by the U.S.S.R., nor have we
any intention of doing so now.
The Estonian community in Canada invite all freedom-loving Canadians to join with them in commemorating this spirit of independence and in demonstrating their desire for liberty and justice in their homeland.
I call upon the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to use all available measures to maintain pressure on the Soviet Union until its illegal occupation of Estonia is ended and that country once again takes her rightful place among the free and independent nations of the world.

Mr. Speaker, the Conservatives have again shown little concern for Canada's tourism industry. In its last Budget the Government again increased the price of gasoline by one-cent a litre. Add this to the two-cent a litre hike in the excise tax announced in September, 1985, the one-cent a litre increase in January,
1987,	and the one-cent a litre hike announced in February, 1987.
These increases, coupled with a 3 per cent hike in the sales tax since 1984, have made gasoline prices in Canada very uncompetitive with our largest tourism customer, the United States. Today the price of gasoline in Canada is over 50 per cent higher than in the U.S. This difference will certainly have a negative effect on the number of American visitors to Canada.
The ever-widening gap in the price of gasoline has prompted the Canadian Automobile Association to state that transportation related industries in Canada will be unable to compete with their American counterparts as we enter a free trade era.
For many regions in the country, tourism is one of the few industries with real growth potential. Tourism has enormous potential for job creation. Why is the Conservative Government attempting to choke off this industry?

subtopic: ACCOMPLISHMENTS OF ATHLETES FROM MISSION-PORT MOODY APPLAUDED
ACCOMPLISHMENTS OF ATHLETES FROM MISSION-PORT MOODY APPLAUDED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 13, Mission-Port Moody sent three athletes to the Olympic Games in Calgary. It is with pride that 1 rise in this House today to congratulate Tracy Wilson and Rob McCall on winning the Bronze Medal for Canada in the pairs ice dance competition. I wish to note that Tracy Wilson is originally from Port Moody, British Columbia, where she spent many years developing the skills and abilities which have served her so well.
In addition, we were able to watch Eden Donatelli capture Canada's second Silver Medal, in the 500-metre short track speed skating competition last night. Eden is from Mission, British Columbia. As well, Kathy Gordon, from Mission, British Columbia, is preparing to compete in the 5,000-metre speed skating event.
Can you imagine, two medal winners and such a great contribution to the Olympics from Mission-Port Moody, British Columbia? Let this House and all Canadians congratulate Mission-Port Moody and these great Canadians.

subtopic: CONTRACT NEGOTIATIONS WITH PUBLIC SERVICE ALLIANCE OF CANADA
CONTRACT NEGOTIATIONS WITH PUBLIC SERVICE ALLIANCE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Public Service employees who are members of the Public Service Alliance of Canada are asking their Members of Parliament why there has been no progress in their contract negotiations. The PS AC has proposed that Treasury Board agree to reduce 31 sets of negotiations to seven to streamline the bargaining talks. Treasury Board has refused, despite savings to the taxpayers which the PSAC estimates at $1.5 million. It is difficult to see why the Government, which claims to be cost conscious, can turn its back on this kind of saving.
Furthermore, the Canada Labour Relations Board recently decided to amalgamate 28 bargaining units at Canada Post into four to gain greater bargaining efficiency. Yet the Government ignores that precedent in its own negotiations.
Why is the Government so deaf to good advice? Because it claims there will be more strikes if bargaining units are consolidated. Yet the Government should know that 95 per cent of negotiations with that union have resulted in negotiated settlements. Why is the Government afraid of efficient public service bargaining? Why does it not get on with the job and deal with the union fairly?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker.
The points I stressed this morning dealt particularly with the failure of the Government to provide a sense of direction and purpose to the country in its industrial policy. I outlined a great many examples across the country, including my own constituency, of shut-downs and lay-offs which had left a great many Canadians in difficult circumstances. I provided some statistics that indicated last year in Ontario alone there were over 100 such shut-downs or significant reductions of staff amounting to well over 14,000 workers.
We are talking about a major pattern of decline throughout the manufacturing sector. It is deindustrialization, a serious weakening of the manufacturing base of our country. As I was saying just before the break, it is almost as if the Government set out to devastate the heart of manufacturing in this country. Unfortunately, there is absolutely nothing in this Budget which provides any sort of beacon of hope for the broad industrial sector in our country.
I say that a counter must be provided which indicates to the industrial manufacturing sector of this country that there is an

February 25, 1988
The Budget-Mr. Gagliano
alternative. I want to quickly lay out a number of points which we feel would give that sector a sense of direction for the future.
First, there has to be a separate ministry of industry. The present experiment of a Ministry of Regional Industrial Expansion, itself detached from the trade functions which have been seconded to external affairs, has been an abysmal failure. There has to be a separate ministry to close this gap and provide us with a sense of direction for the future.
Second, legislation has to be passed to permit communities and workers to review closures in their community. It should not be possible for a plant to simply shut down, pack its bags and head back to the U.S. with no explanation. There should be a careful, considered review with the possibility of buy-out provisions being available to workers in the plant affected in order to maintain a viable operation.
Third, there has to be adjustment legislation, especially for that vast range of workers who are no longer young, or who are not in the special categories of textiles and footwear and clothing which do have provisions for older workers. Such an adjustment procedure was promised by the Minister of Labour as far back as two years, yet nothing has been done through actual legislation.
There has to be as well support for serious research and development efforts in the industrial sector. In addition, our energy sector has to be used to provide a base of support for a viable, dynamic industrial sector. The energy sector cannot simply be seen as a pipeline to the U.S. to help their manufacturing sector increase its dynamism. Instead, we need to use our own base of support in the energy sector to help our own manufacturing enterprises.
We also need an industrial support program, which would be the industrial segment of the 1RDP. At this stage it is aimed mostly at regional development, which is important and significant, but we cannot ignore the fact that there is a tremendous need for modernization of our industrial complex in order to give it hope for the future of being competitive internationally.
We also need to take directions which give potential for Governments to work out planning agreements with some of the larger scale enterprises in this country through which those enterprises can make commitments to important new areas of economic activity, important new industries, which can become sources of exports, of dynamic expansion, and jobs in the future.
We also need sector trade plans, not this across-the-board trade deal which is going to so devastate the industrial sector, like the Auto Pact which has proved so successful and which should be replicated in areas like apparels and chemicals.
Finally, we need a made-in-Canada interest rate policy which keeps interest rates at a lower level than they presently are in order to encourage investment in the industrial sector.
We need a reborn Canada Development Corporation which would be able to help in the development of some of these new areas of activity that are so crucial to a competitive and dynamic Canada in the future. If we do this we can give direction to the industrial future of the country. That is what the country needs for its future jobs, its future exports, and its future as an independent nation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to make my contribution to the debate on the Budget Speech, if we can call it a speech, considering the self-congratulatory exercise indulged in by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), during which he failed to announce a single program or plan reflecting a vision of Canada's future. At this point I would like to quote the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau), our financial critic, who said, and I quote:
The Minister of Finance is much more like an accountant trying to balance his budget than a manager of the Canadian economy with a vision of the future. Yet, the first responsibility of a government should be to govern the country and to prepare for the future; to ensure that our young people will have the education they need to face future difficulties; to guarantee that our workers have and will receive the training they need to adjust to their fast changing working environment; to ensure that our businesses have and will continue to have access to the financial services, the capital and the technology necessary to develop; and finally, to see to it that the poorest members of our society have and will continue to have enough money to live decently.
Mr. Speaker, my hon. colleague hit the right notes in his response to the Minister's speech, but unfortunately the Minister of Finance did not make a Budget Speech. His speech was about the Government's record.
"Bilan d'un echec" (A Statement of Failure) is the title of an article by Alain Dubuc that appeared in La Presse the day after the Budget, on February 11. Mr. Dubuc said, and I quote:
"Last night, Minister of Finance Michael Wilson brought down his fourth Budget. Let's hope it will be his last. On his fourth time around, he dashed any lingering hopes that his Government would be able to deliver the budgetary goods".
Mr. Speaker, those were not the words of the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) nor those of the Liberal Finance critic. This was not a political statement. This was said by a reporter with the newspaper La Presse, well known for his articles on economic affairs. He said he hoped this would be the Government's last Budget and that the Government had failed to deliver the budgetary goods.
Mr. Speaker, whichever way we look at the figures, it is obvious the Government has completely missed the boat.
First of all, as far as the deficit is concerned, Mr. Dubuc explains it all very clearly when he says:
The drop from 38 to 29 billion is largely due to a change in accounting methods. If the same definitions had been used under Liberals, the deficit would have dropped from 36 to 31 billion over the same period . . .
February 25, 1988

Mr. Speaker, if we add to that the $22 billion in tax increases the Minister of Finance has imposed on Canadians, today's deficit should be $14 billion. And if we consider the drop in interest rates, which has reduced the cost of servicing the national debt, the deficit would be lower still. However, our deficit is still around $30 billion. Mr. Speaker, after a period of economic growth, we have still failed to deal with our Budget problems. Nevertheless, in his Speech the Minister of Finance would have us believe that all is well and that we are on the right track.

If having close to $300 billion of national debt after six years of economic recovery is being on the right track, our kids should think seriously about what they must do with the Government, because we are definitely in a real mess and have a real problem. If we cannot reduce our deficit when our economy is good, how are we going to reduce it when we run into economic problems? The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) did not address that problem. In his speech he proposed nothing new, he did not propose what the Canadian vision will be in the coming years.

However, Mr. Speaker, I would like to refer to and list- because Canadians should be reminded of this-all the tax increases imposed by this Government. And when we speak of $22 billion this is a fact, not rhetoric. Let me take a few minutes to illustrate.
First, indirect taxes-sales tax increases. From 9 to 10 per cent on October 10, 1984, Mr. Speaker, their first move. This cost $1 billion. Another increase in indirect taxes, the sales tax-from 10 to 11 per cent on January 1st, 1986. Another $1 billion, Mr. Speaker. And again, a sales tax increase from 11 to 12 per cent on April 1st, 1986. Another $1 billion, Mr. Speaker. Then the sales tax was extended to candies, soda pops, snacks and chips, on June 1st, 1985, another $400 million, and on July 1st, 1987, another $60 million, Mr. Speaker. A sales tax increase from 8 to 12 per cent on paint, wallpaper and toys on January 1st, 1988, another $60 million, Mr. Speaker. Excise tax increased on gas, 2 cents a litre, on September 3, 1985-total $900 million. One cent per litre on January 1st, 1987,-another $450 million. One cent per litre on February 19, 1987,-another $450 million. And of course we had the famous Budget on February 10, again one cent per litre, which will bring another $450 million into Government coffers, Mr. Speaker.
Sales tax equalization on leaded and unleaded fuel, April 1st, 1987-$30 million. Progressive tax increases on air travel, May 1st, 1986-another $55 million. Duties on spirit and tobacco, first increase on May 4, 1985-$340 million; second increase on February 27, 1986-$150 million; third increase on February 19, 1986-$70 million; and fourth increase on January 1st, 1988-$175 million, Mr. Speaker.
The Budget-Mr. Gagliano
There is also the 10 percent tax on long distance calls and cable TV. Imagine, Mr. Speaker, what that means for people in rural communities! They are losing there Post Offices, and in addition they now have to pay tax on long distance calls, when we know very well that in a city environment a long distance call often is essential. But now the Minister of Finance is taxing long distance calls, bringing into his coffers $945 million, Mr. Speaker. The sales tax transfer to wholesalers on July 1st, 1988, in that famous Budget we just had on February 10 will bring another $300 million.
Quietly, the Minister of Finance is proceeding to implement phase two of his tax reform, the value-added tax Canadians said they wanted no part of, and now, for the first time, the Minister of Finance, even though the consultation process is not complete, is transfering the sales tax to wholesalers, which will cost Canadians $300 million. Those tax increases do not include the new sales tax the Government intend to introduce after the next elections.
Mr. Speaker, we should not forget either the Government tried to introduce a tax on food. Thanks to the Opposition who during the summer organized demonstrations and petitions, this Governement backed down, and now it is saying it will be looking at that. It is not done yet, but when he introduced his fiscal reform, the first phase, the Minister of Finance promised in the House that there would not be tax on food.
Mr. Speaker, there are also direct taxes. The deindexing of family allowances, personal exemptions and tax brackets as of January 1st, 1986: $635 million. Cancellation of tax rebate, January 1st, 1986: $650 million. Cancellation of Registered Home-ownership Savings Plan, May 22nd, 1985: $105 million. Temporary surtaxes of 5 and 10 per cent for high income earners, July 1st, 1985 to December 31 st, 1986: $500 millions. General and permanent surtax of 3 per cent for all taxpayers, July 1st, 1986: $1.2 billion. Changes in the way dividends are treated, January 1st, 1986: $300 million. Changes in exemptions for married individuals: $20 millions. We could go on and on.
I just wanted to show how, in three and a half years, this Government has been able to extract $22 billion in taxes while it is bragging about reducing the deficit. After collecting $22 billion in taxes it is still carrying a $30 billion deficit, even though it also benefitted from lower interest rates and, consequently, lower servicing charges for the national debt.
The Budget of February 10 will mark the day in history that the Conservative Government gave up any pretense of trying to close the increasing gap between the rich and the poor in this country. The Mulroney administration cheers so loudly for the few who have prosperity in our society that it is unable to hear the shouts of the many who have not shared in the nation's economic recovery.

February 25, 1988
The Budget-Mr. Gagliano
The Government has turned its back on our youth, our aged, our homeless, our poor and on regional economic disparities. How can the Government be proud of a Budget that refuses to place even a minimum tax on the 60,000 profitable corporations in Canada and at the same time imposes new and increasing taxes which will take over $2 billion out of the pockets of Canadian taxpayers?
Since the Conservatives were elected in 1984, individual Canadians have been forced to pay an additional $22 billion in new taxes. Corporations, by contrast, have only paid $2.6 billion in new taxes. The Budget of February 10 is an economic blueprint for a two-Canada concept of government. It is a blueprint of a Canada for the privileged few who prosper while the rest of the nation are ignored in the corridors of Conservative power.
The Liberal Party believes that Canada is a generous nation and that Canadians of every income group will reject the cynical blueprint for our country.

Madam Speaker, after the Budget and the deficit, I would like, now, to talk about small businesses.
What has this Government done in the last three and a half years to assist that dynamic sector which is the mainspring of our economy? Only one thing, Madam Speaker. The only thing this Conservative government has done for small businesses is to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act in order to make it less accessible to those who really need it, Canadians starting their own business.
Madam Speaker, we had a Small Businesses Loans Act which allowed Canadians wishing to start a business and unafraid of risks to get from our financial institutions a loan totally guaranteed by the Government and to create much needed jobs in our country and our economy.
So, to make sure that all those young people . .. anybody who didn't have the necessary capital to start a business could still get a government guaranteed loan and avoid problems with collateral and guarantees required by the banks.
Madam Speaker, this government's first gesture was to reduce that guarantee to 85 per cent and now people trying to start a business and needing capital must have 15 per cent collateral above what is given, the 20 per cent cash they need to buy equipment, capital assets and other tools required to operate their business.
Madam Speaker, for years we stressed the possibility of a one-stop service for small businesses, so as to group in a single place all informations and programs pertaining to the various levels, municipal, provincial, federal, national, local, and so on, a place where one could inquire and receive the appropriate informations.
A previous Liberal Government had already put forward a project to that effect. Canadians, however, as they were entitled, chose to elect a new Government in September 1984,
and this Conservative Governement launched a consultation process at the beginning of 1985, to find out what the needs of small businesses were in that area. Consultations have now been completed, not without a cost, I am sure, but after three and a half years we are still waiting for specific measures to help the development of small businesses.
There is no program whatsoever regarding such a one-stop service. No financing system that would bring more funds to an area so vital and, yet, so fragile.
Everybody agrees that what small businesses lack the most is precisely good financing sources. Thus, it is important that the federal Government support programs that would help businesses find the necessary start-up funds.
It is useful to recall every now and then that small businesses have created 80 per cent of the jobs in Canada. However, if the small businesses sector were more active, more aggressive, we would have had even more jobs created and, consequently, unemployment would be lower and we would have a far more dynamic economy.
But once again, this government by advocating its philosophy of laissez faire, allows big corporations to grow while small businesses are getting smaller without any aid or relief program.
Madam Speaker, for example, this Governnment after three years and a half has not introduced any consultation program, any program for trading firms to enable small businesses to market their products and services. On the contrary, with respect to tax reform which has now become a law of the land since December last, the Minister of Finance completely ignored the needs of small businesses. We know quite well that 75 per cent of the manufacturing sector in Canada is made up of small businesses.
Madam Speaker, the only sector whose tax rates have been increased under tax reform is precisely that of the small business. Indeed, at present small manufacturing businesses pay 10 per cent of income tax. When the tax reform is implemented, small manufacturing companies will pay 12 per cent, that is 2 per cent more. It is ridiculous and incredible, Madam Speaker, to do that to a dynamic sector which creates 80 per cent of all jobs. And yet the Minister of Finance, who thinks that he has solved all problems in Canada, has never replied to the questions and has never justified why income tax rates in any other sector have not been increased under the tax reform. However, the tax rates of small manufacturing businesses are increased by 2 per cent and the Minister of Finance has been unwilling to justify that increase. There is not a single Canadian, Madam Speaker, who can justify such an increase.
This is not all. It is quite fine, Madam Speaker, for the Government to speak of free trade with the United States. The other day I met a businessman who told me: "Of course, it is
February 25, 1988

quite well for you to say that we will sell our products and services to the United States. At the same time, the Minister of Finance under his tax reform is reducing representation allowances by 20 per cent. Flow do you want me to be represented?" I told him: "Are you going to sell a car or an airplane over there and 20 per cent of those expenditures will not be deductible?" Are small businesses encouraged? Are they encouraged to sell in the United States? Or is it just mere rethoric? The down-to-earth people, Madam Speaker, must always foot the bill, always work harder and harder to pay for some follies of this Government.
We only have to look at the statistics on small businesses' exportations that indicate that 4 percent. . . Madam Speaker, you are telling me that my time is up. I am just about finished. As a matter of fact, I wanted to point out that important matter. Four percent of Canadian exports are made directly by small businesses. That is a very small percentage. Suppose the government would announce some export financing program or a scheme that could really enable our ambassies abroad to help out our small businesses. And suppose that such a program would encourage specialized trading firms abroad to pool products and services offered by small businesses, we could improve significantly that percentage of exports and thus create more employment and make Canada more prosperous.

February 25, 1988
Adjournment Debate

I will give an example. In the United States, it took fourteen years to the postal service before it could balance its books. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am delighted today to take part in this debate on the Budget brought down by my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), on February 10.
If I may, I wish to take a few moments to mention some of the positive achievements that have been accomplished during the time that he has been the Minister of Finance in this Government.
Surely the two most important areas that the Government has succeeded in, where the previous Government failed and failed miserably, have been the lowering of both interest and unemployment rates. In fact, Canada is ranked number one among major industrialized countries in economic growth and job creation. Indeed, more than 1.1 million new jobs have been created in Canada. Of course, 85 per cent of those jobs are
February 25, 1988

full-time. At least half are managerial and professional occupations of a permanent nature.
Interest rates have come way down. In fact, mortgage rates are 3 per cent lower, saving home owners $1,200 a year on a $50,000 mortgage amortized over 25 years. That is money in the householder's pocket. Housing starts have reached a 10-year high. Consumer and investor spending has increased. All of a sudden Canadians have found a new confidence in the Government.

Our Government has restored their confidence.

This record of achievement did not happen by itself. Quite the contrary, this economic reformation was carefully planned and executed, as is clearly spelled out in the Government's agenda for economic renewal which we presented in the House immediately after being elected in November, 1984.
In speaking of the successes that we have nurtured over the past four years, I wish to point out the backbone of our approach which has been responsible for the regeneration of the economy. First, our policy orientations are right on. Fiscal responsibility, tax reform, enhanced trading relationships, regional development, increased equality for women, francophone and minority groups, and regulatory reform have all formed the bulwark of our plan for this nation. They are working not only because they are well planned and executed, but because we are consulting and have consulted with Canadians on the programs that they would like to see. We are listening and we are acting, and our programs and policies are clearly successful.
Within the context we are also committed to fiscal responsibility. Gone are the days when the Government could want only throw away taxpayers' dollars, heaping more dollars on projects which were not proper projects in the first place. The controls in place and the process for justifying government programs are very strict. Few Governments around the world have accorded the same integrity to public expenditures as we have.
Next, we are committed to doing things in priority. Obviously, certain areas take precedence over others. We have priorized the issues which are of greatest concern to Canadians and have and are devoting special attention to those areas. For example, regional development, research and development, and trade enhancement are only a few.
Finally, the Government has a vision for the future, one where all Canadians will reap the benefit of their labours and where the standard of living will be high and all citizens will be proud once again to call themselves Canadian.
I wish to expand on some of the areas I have touched upon and which form part of our over-all plan.
It is absolutely essential, if this country is to recover, that we revitalize the private sector and position Canada's economy to
The Budget-Mr. Merrithew
meet the challenge of international competition in the 1990s. The key behind this has been the modernization of the regulatory environment for business. We have deregulated energy, the transportation sectors, opened up the financial markets to global opportunities, and stimulated greater competition in financial services. We are updating the outdated legislation for competition policy, copyrights, and patents. We have not stopped there. One of the highest priorities has been to privatize some of our Crown corporations which no longer have any reason to be government controlled.
I invite the Opposition to have a look at the success of those privatizations since we have taken that action.
Tax reform is another major initiative of the Government. It will come into effect in stages over the next year. As early as this summer it will mean less taxes being paid by the average Canadian, and a fairer distribution of the tax burden across the country.
Indeed the federal income tax system has been formed to help both businesses and individuals compete in the world. Hand in hand with this new approach to a fairer taxation system is the major effort to control government spending. Nothing is more basic to a strong framework for private sector growth and job creation than responsible management of government finances.
In 1984 the federal deficit and the national debt were almost out of control. In the mid-1970s a former Auditor General said that the Government lost control of the public purse-strings. Indeed spending was out of control. Not so with our Government.
Our first priority was to get government spending under control. Through team effort and under the leadership of the Minister of Finance we have been able to do so to a certain extent. The deficit has been systematically reduced. For the current fiscal year we will meet our previously announced target of $29.3 billion. We must remember that in 1984 the deficit was better than $37 billion and rising. In continuing our attack on the deficit, we have not lost sight of the day when the Budget can be balanced.
Another major area of government effort has been to enhance our trade opportunities abroad, with all countries around the world. However, since we have a natural, historic trading relationship with our largest partner, the United States, we have pursued a special arrangement to open up access to that great market-place to the south. We have succeeded in negotiating a comprehensive free trade agreement with our American neighbours, which I think will lead to a more efficient economy, better able to compete in the international market-place. More jobs will be created as Canadians realize the immense benefits and opportunities which are now available through our trading savvy south of the border. We estimate that there will be a net increase of at least 120,000 new jobs in 1993.

February 25, 1988
The Budget-Mr. Merrithew
1 want to speak for a moment, if I may, of those things in the Budget which relate to the forestry and mines portfolio that comes under my responsibility. The Government has a good relationship with both the forestry and mining industries and communities. After consultations with the mining industries it was decided to widen the definition of a mineral resource to include kaolin under the Income Tax Act. This will allow the mineral to receive the favourable tax treatment which the federal Government provides to the mineral industry.
Since interest in kaolin deposits has been shown in the West, this will be a further boost to regional development in that region, providing they take advantage of the new regulatory regime.
Another positive note for the forestry and mining industries is that with the necessary increase of one cent per litre in the excise tax on gasoline, primary resource producers as well as farmers and fishermen can continue to collect the fuel tax rebate, ensuring that they are not affected by the increase. Additionally there was no increase in tax on diesel fuel. The Minister of Finance has clearly recognized the importance of maintaining cost competitiveness of Canadian minerals and forest products in export markets by not increasing the excise tax on diesel fuel for transportation.
There are two other measures which I will mention. The Budget reaffirmed the need for special assistance for certain users of energy consumption equipment, including primary producers, through the mechanism of the capital cost allowance. This incentive for investment will continue to provide assistance to the forest and mining sectors.
The national labour sponsored venture capital corporations provision is another part of the Budget. First introduced on May 23, 1985, the Budget adds a new measure which allows individuals a federal tax credit of 20 per cent of the cost of shares acquired in 1988 and subsequently. The maximum individual federal tax credit remains at $700 per annum. This should provide a significant source of new equity capital for small and medium-sized businesses in the forest sector by giving workers an opportunity to invest in and benefit from the profitability of their own companies.
One issue in which I have been interested as a Maritimer is regional development. As a Minister and a Member of Parliament from New Brunswick, I want to deal with that particular issue for just a few moments.

I turn now to regional development. This is an important matter to me as a Minister and a Member from New Brunswick.
Our Government has shown and will continue to show it is committed to the Atlantic region.
f English]
The Government has demonstrated and will continue to demonstrate its special attention to programs for the region in which I live in Atlantic Canada. Of course we recognize that the programs and policies of the previous federal Government were not working and that unemployment rates were unbelievably and cruelly high in the Atlantic region. The Government has embarked upon a new course, a clear departure from the laissez-faire attitude of the previous Government.
We have created the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency which has unprecedented powers to nurture and assist development in the region. This did not come out of thin air. We on this side of the House listened to and consulted with Atlantic Canadians. They told us that they wanted a new approach, one that would work, would be based in the region, and would have a sensitivity toward Atlantic Canadian problems and aspirations. This did not escape us. We have created ACOA to provide this focus for development in the region and this window for the federal Government to contribute marginally to prosperity in Atlantic Canada.
It is important to note that it is the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who has taken the lead role in providing stronger commitment to and clear vision of the needs of Atlantic Canadians. Test we forget what has happened to date on that particular issue, I was just given the figures today of expenditures under ACOA in three categories in the region covering the four provinces. To date, under the Atlantic Enterprise Program, IRDP, and ERDA, we have approved 558 applications and authorized ACOA contributions of some $76,497,000.
What has this brought about? It has brought about an estimated total project cost-that means new capital investments in our region-of $229 million in Atlantic Canada. We think that is fairly important and fairly significant.
Created in June of last year and carefully designed, with legislation currently moving through the House, ACOA is moving on all fronts to approve projects which will benefit the region. The actions of the Government have meant jobs in Atlantic Canada.
Earlier this week the Hon. Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin) tried to say, unbelievably, that employment rates in eight provinces are higher today than they were at the height of the recession. The truth of the matter is that eight provinces have lower unemployment rates than in December, 1982 when the Canadian unemployment rate was at its highest. When unemployment began to decline somewhat in 1983 in Ontario and Quebec, the rate in Atlantic Canada and the West continued to rise. For example, the unemployment rate in Newfoundland, Saskatchewan, and Alberta reached its highest point, not in December, 1982, the depths of the recession, but in September, 1984. The highest rate in my province, the Province of New Brunswick, was in January, 1985.
February 25, 1988

In Atlantic Canada the unemployment rate did not begin to recover until after the 1984 election. It took a Progressive Conservative Government to reverse the negative trend of unemployment in Atlantic Canada, which had been the trademark of the previous Government. All provinces across Canada, except P.E.I., now have lower unemployment rates than in September, 1984.
May I just take a moment to deal with the statements of Hon. Members of the New Democratic Party opposite, while calling upon the Government for more regional development, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) has made his priorities clear. He said:
Top priorities would be to keep the economy running well in central Canada,
where the continental mechanism has been very effective.
In fact, the NDP Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) went a step further by asserting, incredibly, that part of the new Navy frigate contract which was recently awarded to the Saint John shipyard in my riding, fair and square to the lowest tenderer, should be split off to Quebec. This is the same Party that argued in the past for procurement contracts to go to the lowest bidder. Now the NDP argues just the opposite, thereby stirring up regional divisions and questions as to the NDPs credibility on these important matters. The people in Saint John and in Atlantic Canada have noted those comments.
In closing, I want to say that this Budget is just part and parcel of the Government's continuing commitment to a prosperous Canada, and a prosperous Atlantic Canada I am proud to say. The next year will be the sixth year of sustained economic expansion in Canada. That, in itself, is unique. It will see the implementation of a number of our priority programs for child care, regional development, science and technology and national defence. We will continue our commitment to the agriculture, energy, fishing, mining and forestry sectors. We will fulfil our commitment to a stronger and more compassionate Canada.
This Budget helps to make this commitment possible. It does it in a careful and responsible way. It proves once again what we have said from the beginning. We have a plan and we have stuck to that plan. That plan is working, it is creating jobs and new opportunities in the area of Canada from which I come. We are cutting the deficit and implementing important policies for all regions of Canada.
I am proud and pleased to speak in support of the Budget brought down by our Minister of Finance on February 10, 1988, because it is one more step in making Canada a better and more prosperous place in which to live, to work and to raise a family.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in rising to address this year's Budget, I want to
begin by looking very briefly at the history of Conservative budget-making in these last number of years. We are now into the fourth year of Conservative Government.
The Government's first economic declaration was a real slasher. Conservatives basically said: "Move over, Margaret Thatcher, we want to show you that we have real Conservatives in Canada, we will have a really tough Conservative Budget". There was slashing of expenditures. There was the slashing of the indexing of family allowances and old age pensions. There were big budget cuts in the environment, whole programs just slaughtered, to show the folks out there that they were really serious as Conservatives about being tough on the Budget.
Arts expenditures were cut, again in spite of absolutely clear promises to the contrary, as promises were made on the sacred trust to the social programs. Arts expenditures were very seriously cut, one of the first casualties of the new slashing Conservative approach to budget-making back in the fall of 1984.
What has happened? Canadians did not like what Conservative Members did. Old age pensioners stood up and fought back. Canadian women who were going to lose the family allowance indexing fought back, unfortunately not as successfully as old age pensioners. Old age pensioners were successful in insisting that indexing not be cut for the old age pension.
Arts groups marched on Ottawa and said: "You had better keep to those promises, we are an important part of Canadian society and we do not want to see expenditures in our area cut". Environmentalists spoke up and insisted that programs for the protection of the environment were a high priority for Canadians. They were right.
This first attack on Budgets was back in the fall of 1984 and the Government had to learn that it would not work, that Canadians really did object. Canadians were not ardent followers of Margaret Thatcher nor were they ardent followers of Ronald Reagan. The Conservative Government preferred these two models of increased expenditures on law and order defence and the military, and cuts in social areas, arts and environmental programs. Conservatives learned that this was not acceptable to Canadians, and I am glad to see that they learned a bit of a lesson.
Instead of these massive slashes, subsequent Budgets have provided for more careful trimmings. Indeed, Conservatives have poured on the fertilizer in other areas. In some areas, there has even been growth.
Here we have the curiosity of a Government that talks about slashing and reducing the deficit, while in fact expenditures are going up. They are going up at a greater rate than economic growth, rising faster than inflation. In short, there have been real increases in expenditures in Canada.
For the first year in our history, there are expenditures in the federal Budget of over $100 billion. For statutory programs, the increases are in the order of 4.6 per cent, for non-
February 25, 1988

statutory programs, there are increases of 3.9 per cent, for total program spending, there are increases of 4.3 per cent, and of course, the expenditures to pay the service charges on the public debt amount to 9.7 per cent, a massive increase. The total budget increase for this year is 5.5 per cent. With inflation at around 4 per cent, we can see that that is a real increase.
The irony is that the Government is talking about reducing the deficit. What are government Members talking about? They are talking about comparing the deficit in the worst of the Trudeau years, the time of a recession, a time when we would expect the deficit to rise if there were to be any humanity at all, a time when the deficit would have to go up or there would have been even more massive suffering than there was, with the deficit now when employment has risen a bit. In comparison with the worst of the Trudeau years, they say that we are reducing the deficit.
In fact, every year the public debt is rising, and it is rising by very substantial figures, around $30 billion a year. We are into the fourth year of a deficit in the order of $30 billion. Of course, the debt charges are rising year after year and yet the Government uses rhetoric about reductions.
Looking at the fine print, we find that there is a reduction in the rate of the increase, not a real reduction in the growth of expenditures. We have to moderate the growth of expenditures, not reduce expenditures altogether. They are still rising. Let us be very clear. We have heard some rhetoric, but the reality is rather different.
The Government is promising tax reform, but what in fact has it actually been doing? It has been increasing taxes for middle and lower income Canadians. There have been massive tax increases in each of the years we have had a Conservative Government. Why is this? For one thing, there are still tax giveaways for better off Canadians. There are still massive loopholes. There are still some 60,000 profitable corporations that are not paying taxes. The Government is still resisting all the recommendations made by my Party and by many Canadians to apply at least a minimum corporate income tax in order to ensure that profitable corporations pay their fair share of taxes. That has not happened.
Corporate income taxes do not bring a very substantial part of the money into the federal Treasury. Projections for this year put personal income tax at $45,410 million and corporate income taxes at only around $12 billion. Unemployment insurance contributions are nearly as high at $10.6 billion. Sales and excise taxes are actually very substantial at $28,855 million. Sales and excise taxes paid by Canadians for this fiscal year are much higher than corporate income taxes. This is of course a very convenient way for the Government to be collecting taxes, but it is not a fair way.
Sales and excise taxes are largely hidden taxes and they are regressive taxes. They are not related to ability to pay, which income tax is. Income tax is progressive, but sales and excise taxes are not. Of course, with the trade deal, there will be a
The Budget-Ms. McDonald
reduction in excise taxes, so again taxes elsewhere will have to go up. There will be some kind of sales tax, but the Government is holding off from telling us exactly what it wants to collect in sales taxes. All we know, or at least we hope we know, is that food will not be included. A whole lot of other items will be.
There are massive increases there because the Government will not come to terms with collecting taxes fairly from people who can afford to pay them. Again, we hear rhetoric about tax reform, but let us be very, very clear about what tax reform actually means. The Government wants to reduce the tax rate. The Government wants to follow in the footsteps of Margaret Thatcher and Ronald Reagan.
There were reductions in the income tax rate, particularly for the wealthy in Britain and in the United States. They were following the trickle-down theory which is that with these kinds of reductions, wealthy people would invest more and jobs would be created. In fact, they have not found that the trickle down theory has actually produced those kinds of jobs. It certainly has not produced justice, equity or harmony in those societies. But that is still the model we have from the Conservative Government.
We have this talk about tax reform but it is just a reduction in the rate. The Government says it still has to collect the same amount of money, but instead of doing it in a fair way through the income tax system which is related to ability to pay, it is going to be collected in an unfair way through hidden taxes, sales taxes, regressive taxes which hit middle and low-income people worse than they hit those with a better ability to pay. The Government talks about a revenue-neutral kind of tax reform. We have to collect the same amount of revenue but we are going to do it in a different way. Is it fair? No, it is not. Tax reform sounds good, it promises reform, but these are in fact regressive measures.
We have a certain amount of ideology in the Budget Papers which the Government has come up with. We have The Fiscal Plan and when you read the fine print there is a lot of reference to percentages. There is also a lot of reference to relating expenditures to the size of the economy, as if government expenditures ought to be a certain proportion of the Gross Domestic Product. This reflects the Conservative ideology that there is a kind of right amount of government, but not too much, we had to have enough to pay for certain social programs, yes, but more than that we do not want. There is some kind of mumbo-jumbo or magic Figure which is the right amount but not too much. This is the ideology. It is not very practical because it obviously depends upon what the money is being spent for. Is it productive? Is it going to improve the capacity of Canadians to create jobs, to use our wealth wisely? Is it going to promote health, education, research and technological development? Yet those are not the kinds of questions being asked. The question asked is simply whether it is being spent by the public sector or the private sector.

February 25, 1988
The Budget-Ms. McDonald
If the private sector puts thalidomide on the market, that is not economic growth. That is disaster. Yet the Government takes this very narrow approach that what the private sector does must be positive for the economy. Yet if the public sector does something to get rid of pollution or promote public health, somehow that is bad because it is being done by the public sector. This kind of ideological blindness on the part of the Government is extremely unfortunate.
I also want to refer to what is not in the Budget. We have a discussion of expenditures projected for the fiscal year and the income the Government expects to get during that fiscal year. To some extent it is related to unemployment or projected employment and economic growth, interest rates, and a few other economic indicators. Yet most of it is just the money coming in and going out of the Government's hands over the year. It is not related to, you might say, the productive capacity of Canadians, the physical plant, the environment, the forests, the soil, the waters, the fisheries or our farmland. We do not have any kind of accounting of that sort. Yet that is the kind of information we should be seeing more often so we can assess where we are going, how productive we are, and whether we are building up our productive capacity or allowing it to deteriorate.

Madam Speaker, some departments are winners and others are losers in this Budget. The Department of the Environment, of which I am the critic for the New Democratic caucus, is a losing department. Even though total Government expenditures will increase, those concerning Environment Canada will be reduced in this fiscal year, in real terms.
The expenditures of that department are reduced against the public's will and despite statements the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) made before the Standing Committee on Environment and Forestry.

We discussed this matter with the Minister and he told us in committee that for environmental protection enforcement purposes: "Suffice it to say that Environment Canada will get 6 to 8 per cent of the $3 million of new money added to the pot for enforcement purposes. For the Department of the Environment the person-years will be in the vicinity of 70 for a total of 125 additional person-years for the same purposes."
When we look at the Estimates, that is not what has happened. In fact, the resources for conservation and protection are down. Total funds have been reduced in real terms. They have not gone up with the cost of living and there is a real difference in absolute terms in the number of person-years.
The Department says there will be 12 new person-years in the Supplementary Estimates, but this means a net reduction of 30 person-years over last year. It has been down by 254 since the Government came into power. A real reduction. This
in an absolutely vitally important area, one where the public wants to see more action on preservation of the environment.
With respect to the wildlife toxicology fund, the Government first let its funding lapse. There was only SI million in the past three years. We do not know if there is going to be any replacement of those funds in any other fashion. The fund had been handling the money when direct departmental expenditures were cut, but we do not know what their funding is going to be.
We have slashes in the environmental budget for nongovernmental organizations, which have played a really vitally important role in defending the environment, giving the public input and using expertise from ordinary citizens who know what is happening to the environment in their particular area. The Government cut $75,000 from their funding since last year. It seems that the annual grant to the Canadian Coalition on Acid Rain has been discontinued. Acid rain is our major environmental problem, and here the coalition dealing very actively and vigorously with this matter is not getting any funding.
I want to address for a couple of minutes the question of the size of the Public Service. Government has made a big to-do about its reduction in the Public Service as a matter of efficiency and productivity. Of course, the plan was announced some time ago for a reduction of 15,000 persons in the Public Service to take place gradually. Here we have in this year's Budget a little bit of bragging by the Government. Implementation will continue and staff reductions to date have resulted in cumulative savings of $375 million by 1990-91. The cumulative savings from the person-years will exceed $1.5 billion, with recurring savings of about $500 million each year.
1 suggest that this is absolute bunk. Presumably they have the numbers right and I am not going to quarrel with that. However, if there were real reductions in expenditures as a result of these cuts in the Public Service we would be seeing a decrease in over-all expenditure. That is not what is happening. Budget expenditures are still going up by 5.5 per cent. You have the civil service going down and expenditures going up. What does that mean? It simply means that we have a Government that likes the rhetoric of cutting down the Public Service and slashing permanent jobs.
These are good jobs held by dedicated public servants. The Government has taken some pleasure in saying, a la Margaret Thatcher and Ronald Reagan, that we are being tough in cutting the Public Service. Yet it is replacing these people by contracting out. It does not save any money. We can see that costs are still going up. What it does mean is that a company gets a contract. Maybe it is a company that is going to hive off a little money in gratitude to the Party in power.
This Budget has the biggest expenditures in our history, over $100 billion in expenditures. We have a so-called ethics
February 25, 1988

package. The Government now claims to be interested in honesty in government, yet there are no reforms in that area.
We have the biggest spending we will ever have, yet we have a tendering process which is full of holes. The Canadian public likes to think that there is a process by which the company with the lowest contract bid that is capable of performing the terms of the contract will get it. In fact, that only counts for some contracts. There is still enormous ministerial discretion in the awarding of contracts in every Department of the Government.
The new ethics package does not address that at all, nor does it address the issue of corporate donations to political Parties which are, of course, the very basis for our kickback system. If you get rid of corporate donations to Parties you cannot have a kickback system. There is nothing to kick back.

speechtext: How about trade unions?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am asked, "How about trade unions?" Well, should there be a trade union that is in the business of selling widgets to the Government in competition with other businesses, it should come under the same rules. However, trade unions are not in the business of selling widgets or any other gadgets to the Government. They are not profitable corporations. They represent workers in contract negotiations for wages and working conditions. They are not in sales, they are not out to make a profit. Should they be doing that, they ought to be treated the same, but why would you treat two organizations with completely different purposes as if they had the same purpose?
In conclusion, the Government does have a program but, unfortunately, it is not the right program. It is going ahead with its cut-backs in the Public Service. Its so-called tax reform is a fraud. It is not dealing with honesty in government. We see lost opportunities. Opportunities to be fair with this Budget and to bring in a minimum corporate income tax are absolutely lost.
The unfairness is continuing. The increase in burden on middle and lower income Canadians is continuing. The day of reckoning will come. These costs will have to be dealt with. You cannot just talk about reducing the deficit and limiting expenditures. Somehow you have to bring them into alignment. That is not happening because the Government will not deal with making those people pay taxes who can afford to do so and thus bring real fairness into the tax system. As long as we do not have that, unfairness will continue and Canadians will be extremely dissatisfied.
I regret that this Budget does not deal with the real problems with which we must deal in our society and with the fairness which Canadians would like to see. I regret that the Government is hiding from these and putting it off to future Governments to come to terms with those real problems.

Madam Speaker, I enjoyed the Member's lecture on how to run the Government and debt. She is very
The Budget-Ms. McDonald
critical and her answer to everything seems to be that we have to spend more money. I wonder whether she and her colleagues would consider doing the people of Manitoba a favour by sitting down with the NDP Government there and having a talk with it about debt and increased taxes. Would they let them know that they are against reducing the civil service? They are reducing the civil service in Manitoba. If it is all right for an NDP Government in Manitoba to do that, it is quite proper here.
Manitoba has had the biggest tax grab in the history of the province. Manitobans are paying an additional $369 million in taxes, a 20 per cent increase. I hope the Member will sit down with Premier Pawley and tell him how disturbed she is. A new tax of 2 per cent on net income has hit taxpayers there. Hydro rates are up by 9.7 per cent. Telephone rates are up by 11.5 per cent. Autopac premiums are up by 9 per cent to 30 per cent. All other government fees are up by an average of 20 per cent, including drivers' licences and birth certificates. An additional 1 per cent sales tax has hit all Manitobans. A land transfer tax has hit Manitoba home buyers. There is a new 7 per cent tax on take-out food and energy conservation materials. Payroll tax has increased by 50 per cent to 2.25 per cent. There is a new water tax.
Each person in Manitoba has a debt load of $9,000. Five years ago it was only $4,500. The history of Manitoba debt is that it took 117 years of government spending to arrive at the present debt. The NDP Government in Manitoba has been responsible for almost half of it in only five years.
I hope the Member will go to Manitoba and have a talk with the Government. The people of Manitoba would be most gratified if the Member would go there and tell them how to run the Government as she has told us how to run the country. Manitobans are the victims of the biggest tax grab in the history of the province. Even though they have to pay more, they will get less.
In addition, Manitobans must face cut-backs in hospital beds, cut-backs in hospital services and closures of wards, and long waiting periods for CAT scans and other diagnostic services. People of Manitoba have to go to the United States to get CAT scans. That is disgraceful. In addition, there is mismanagement in the protection of children.
I will give some examples of mismanagement by the NDP. As a result of the mix-up between Manitoba Telephones and Saudi Arabia, $27 million was lost. Manitoba forest industries have lost $31 million. Manitoba Public Insurance Corporation has lost $58 million. Flyer Industries has lost $100 million, and workers' compensation has lost $148 million. Flyer Industries was a Crown corporation which the Manitoba Government sold. NDP Members in the House criticize the Government for getting rid of unproductive Crown corporations, but I do not hear them saying anything about the NDP Government in Manitoba. It is all right for it to dispose of Crown corporations. The NDP Government intends to establish another Crown corporation, another mix-up there.

February 25, 1988
The Budget-Ms, McDonald
Would the Hon. Member be kind enough, when criticizing the federal Government, also to include the NDP Government in Manitoba? Would she pass along her comments on how she would straighten out the ungodly mess in Manitoba? A population of a million people cannot carry that debt load in Manitoba or put up with such mismanagement. Would the Member give her commitment that she will speak to the NDP Government and get it to start straightening out the mess in Manitoba before being so critical of the federal Government?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there are quite a few items on the list the Hon. Member has asked me to address. 1 will try to deal with most of them. First, I did not at any time say that we should spend more, more, more, more, more. I was pointing out the contradictions between a government which talks about reducing the deficit but, rather, has increased the public debt in the order of $30 billion every year for four years. Added up, that is roughly $120 billion in increases in the public debt since the Conservatives came to power.
The best example of reductions in the public debt is Saskatchewan. Over a period of 20 years the first CCF Government, under Tommy Douglas, reduced not only the deficit, which is the difference in expenditures and revenues per year, but the accumulated public debt. That was done by the first CCF Government in Canada.
It is true that there have been increases in the deficit in Manitoba. There have been in every province of the country as there have been in the federal Government. They are associated with the time of the recession. The years of 1981-82 were particularly bad. Manitoba is not out of line with other provinces. In Saskatchewan a CCF Government completely disposed of the public debt which was built up by the Conservatives. It was built up again by the Conservatives, reduced again by the NDP, and has now been built up again by the Conservatives.
The lesson is exactly the opposite to what the Hon. Member suggests. There was actually the accomplishment of reduction in the public debt in a CCF-NDP province. There are increases in Manitoba, but they are no worse than in any other province and no worse than what has been happening federally.
There are inconsistencies in the Hon. Member's remarks about increased taxes in Manitoba. He cannot have it both ways. He complains about the debt in Manitoba and he complains when taxes are increased to deal with that debt. That Government is being consistent and is trying to deal with this debt. They were fair tax increases, and that is the big difference with the Pawley Government. It has increased some taxes but it has done it fairly and has related it to ability to pay. That is what the federal Government is not doing. It has not brought in a minimum corporate income tax, and taxes have increased disproportionately for middle and lower income Canadians.
Those two Governments face a problem and one of those Governments, the Government of Manitoba, has approached it fairly. The federal Conservative Government has not approached it fairly.
The Hon. Member referred to health care services and difficulties in the health care field. He ought to look next door to Saskatchewan with its Conservative Government. There has been an appalling deterioration in health care services there. It is the same in British Columbia with, in effect, a conservative Government, a Social Credit Government. Health care services come under established program financing where we had cutbacks federally. It is the same for post-secondary education. Therefore, part of the problems the provinces have in paying for their health care costs stem from the fact that the Conservative Government has cut back financing for those very programs.
I do not think the Member is at all consistent or fair in what he has to say in making comparisons between Manitoba and the federal Government.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I wonder if the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) would care to comment on ways of raising taxes that are more fair and consistent? I note that in the past, Canada's tax system has tended to impose taxes less heavily on those corporations that have garnered extremely high profit margins. I have some Statistics Canada figures from 1983-and I realize we had a Liberal Government then-which show that the 25 largest business entities in the country, which control one-third of our entire $717 billion corporate pie, although their profit rates were extremely high, generally fell into one of the lowest tax rates, averaging something in the neighbourhood of 9.6 per cent of actual taxes paid on their profits, compared to small corporations which were paying an average of 17.1 per cent at the same time. The results seem to be that the tax system encourages the very large corporations not only to avoid supporting Government but to use the profits and savings from not paying taxes to raid the smaller and medium-sized corporations, putting them out of business. Does the Hon. Member think this is a good way to create economic development?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, Madam Speaker, it is certainly not a good thing for the economy to have this happen. We know that it is the small and medium-sized businesses that are creating jobs in Canada. They also happen to be the ones which are relatively highly taxed. The Hon. Member is indeed correct in talking about the enormous tax advantages the larger corporations have.
