speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am indeed pleased that I have the opportunity to be involved in this debate this afternoon. I will take this opportunity to be perhaps somewhat more positive about the country in which we live than the Member who spoke previously. I would like to talk about our country's future and the capability of its citizens.
I do have a sense of responsibility, being a Member of this place, to share in the positive news about what is happening in Canada without dwelling continuously on the past days of previous administrations and the sort of problems we would have had to face should a Liberal-NDP coalition have continued. Fortunately for Canadians, that did not happen.
The night the Budget was tabled, the pundits labelled it dull, stand-pat and stay-the-course. The inference was not complimentary. However, I would suggest that there could not have been a greater compliment. We are staying the course because it is a strategy that works and has been proven to work. Why would we want to veer from a winning formula? Why would we want to return to the days of budget trickery and gimmickry that dazzled Canadians with seductive but ultimately costly programs, of promises and more promises? Why would we want to return to those days of sky-high unemployment, escalating inflation, crippling interest rates, unprecedented deficit growth, plummeting dollar values, declining economic growth and crumbling investor confidence? Why would we want to do that? It is a stay-the-course Budget which allows individuals, along with the business community, to know that the solid record of progress will continue and will provide for a stronger, more competitive, more prosperous and more innovative Canada.
When this Government came into office, the Minister of Finance outlined the Government's commitment to moving Canada away from a decade of soaring government deficits,
The Budget-Mr. Corbett
rising unemployment and sluggish uncertain growth. The Government was committed to taking the lead in economic renewal. However, the Minister of Finance warned that renewal would not come quickly, nor would it be easy. There are no quick fixes. It would have to be undertaken in a deliberate, well thought out program. The Minister of Finance issued the challenge. We must put our fiscal house in order. We must redefine the role of Government so it provides a better framework for growth and job creation. We must develop policies that will foster higher investment, greater innovation and increased international competition. We must do these things in a manner which is fair, open and consistent with the spirit of Canadianism.
Three-and-a-half years later, Canadians are enjoying the benefits outlined in the economic agenda of November, 1984. That agenda set the course for the economic renewal and revitalization that this nation has witnessed and been a part of since that period.
This Government took office and took hold of an economy that was-my colleague from St. John was rather kind, I think, when he said it was almost out of control. I will not be quite as kind. I will say that it was out of control. All Canadians have enjoyed greater prosperity since that time. In my home Province of New Brunswick, a total of 33,000 jobs have been created since 1984. I am confident that under this Government and the steady hand of the Minister of Finance, the significant job creation in New Brunswick will continue.
This Government has more good news for New Brunswick-ers. In December, 1987, in the neighbouring constituency of the Hon. Minister of State for Forestry and Mines (Mr. Merrithew) the inflation rate in Saint John was only 3.7 per cent, below the national average of 4.2 per cent for the same period. That is significant. If my colleagues opposite do not think it is, then they should go to Saint John and ask Saint Johners how significant or insignificant they think it to be.
The personal disposable incomes of New Brunswickers increased in 1986 by 4.4 per cent. It is expected that they will increase by 6.4 per cent when the 1987 figures are released.
The number of families living below the poverty line has decreased in New Brunswick from 18.5 per cent to 15.5 per cent, a three point reduction between 1984 and 1985. That is in just one year's time. We know that it is still too high, but the Government has taken initiatives to deal with that intolerable situation with which we were left from previous administrations. The programs are working well.
The list of good news is long. The amount of prosperity and good news is directly proportionate to the depth of the Government's commitment to New Brunswick and to all of Atlantic Canada. It is important to note the Government's commitment to regional economic development in Atlantic Canada. This commitment was reinforced in the Budget.

February 25, 1988
The Budget-Mr. Corbett
Throughout the tenure of the present administration it has been a priority.
The most significant initiative to date is the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. This new agency has its headquarters in Atlantic Canada. It is administered by Atlantic Canadians. It makes only good sense that those who deal with the problems which are unique to our region be people who know what the problems are. After all, when one's car breaks down one does not take it to Oshawa or Detroit to have it fixed. One has it serviced nearby where there is a competent level of expertise and ability to deal with the problems. We have a good sense Government, and this is a good sense Budget.
ACOA will handle a total of $1.05 billion over five years to encourage small and medium-size businesses and industry in the Atlantic region. ACOA is not the only initiative that has been taken by the Government in Atlantic Canada. There is in addition to it the Atlantic Enterprise Program, the Atlantic Opportunities Program, Enterprise Cape Breton, the economic and regional development agreements, six of which are in New Brunswick alone, plus initiatives for forestry, agriculture, energy, fisheries, investment, mining and small craft harbours. This is only the tip of the iceberg in terms of regional development in our part of the country.
The Canadian Jobs Strategy is working to create new training and employment opportunities in the Atlantic provinces. Jobs, jobs, jobs are indeed being created.
In 1984 the Government committed itself to social justice. A high priority of the Government was to restructure the tax system. The tax reform initiatives announced in 1987 have gone a long way to accomplishing this commitment. Again, in a part of the country where regional disparity has too long been a way of life this is significant.
There are now some 86,000 low-income earners who will no longer pay any income tax. There will be in excess of 875,000 low and middle-income earners in Atlantic Canada who will pay less income tax because of the tax reform system. We never hear about these measures from the socially conscious and aware people who apparently maintain that these people do not exist. Collectively, New Brunswickers will pay 5.8 per cent less of the tax burden on a national scale. This is good news for New Brunswickers and for Atlantic Canadians.
Income tax cuts will mean more money left in the pockets of Atlantic Canadians. The more money that we have the more we will spend and invest. The more money we spend and invest the more that will remain in Atlantic Canada to create the economic growth and the much needed jobs that the Government is committed to working toward.
Like all things everything cannot be perfect. We cannot have everything that we would like to have. In this respect I would like to leave one thought with the Government. It is with reference to some concerns that my constituents have expressed about the 15 per cent tax on investment income.
Canadians believe that all individuals and corporations must pay their fair share of taxes. Obviously, that is a primary consideration of the tax reform proposals. Unfortunately, what is happening now is that many Canadians feel themselves paying the cost of this effort. The modification of the original proposal was an apparent effort to meet both the needs of Canadians and the need for tax fairness. However, many people in my constituency of Fundy-Royal continue to appeal to the Minister to withdraw the investment income tax proposal in order to protect the future value of their insurance policies. I urge the Government to consider seriously some way of ensuring that these people's fears are allayed.
Allow me to stray for a moment, Madam Speaker, to the free trade agreement. This historic agreement is the fulcrum of Canada's prospects for our continued economic prosperity in the future. This trade agreement will provide better and expanded opportunities for economies of scale in Canadian production and marketing. The Canada-U.S. trade agreement will stimulate innovation, greater productivity and lead Canadians to a lower-cost economy. My main concern as a parent with the Canada-U.S. trade agreement is that it will result in secure future growth and better opportunities for our children and their children. What opponent of this agreement is prepared to stand in his or her place to deny their children the right to a better future?
New Brunswick and the Atlantic provinces have long been denied access to their traditional and geographic trading partners along the Atlantic seaboard. As a matter of fact it was in the days of the national policy that we were first denied this natural trading route. Since then it has been a downhill slide for Atlantic Canada.
Our geographic natural partners along the Atlantic seaboard have been denied to us for too long. The New England market is vast. With unimpeded access to such a market Atlantic Canadians will be able to enjoy once again the prosperity of times past. We in Atlantic Canada should be clamouring for the heads of those who would deny us access to our traditional and geographic trading partners. We have been suffering for too long the consequences of such measures as countervails on softwood lumber, the proposed countervail on potash and the countervails on fish and potatoes. The list goes on and on. Those who would deny us the opportunity to rid ourselves of those millstones around our necks should indeed go to New Brunswick, to Atlantic Canada, to suggest that we as Atlantic Canadians should not have these opportunities. I would welcome the opportunity of having somebody go into the region to say so.
Exports from New Brunswick to the United States accounted for 15 per cent of employment in New Brunswick and a total of $2.6 billion annually.
Atlantic Canada has been battered in the war of protectionism between Canada and America on many different occasions. The workers and businessmen of the region want an end
February 25, 1988

to this. They want that end to be the culmination of a Canada-U.S. trade agreement.
All Canadians want the 120,000 new jobs that this agreement will bring about by as early as 1993. That is just the tip of the iceberg. There are a great many studies in the works and others which are in place which suggest that eventually we will be looking at something more significant and substantial than just 120,000 jobs.
Canadians want their real family incomes to increase by $1,800 annually as a result of this deal. Canadian consumers want better quality. They want better selection and lower prices. They want the U.S.-Canada trade agreement.
The implementation of this deal will cost Canadians little. It will take courage and a strong commitment to a better future and the desire to see our nation strong. That is all that Canadians will have to pay for this agreement. It is a small price.
I suggest that in 20 years from now we in Canada will be hard pressed to find a single living soul including our socialist friends and their allies in the Liberal Party who will say that they were against the deal. The same was true with respect to the Auto Pact.
[DOT] <1710)
What is the reason for the prosperity? What is the cause for all of the good news in Atlantic Canada? The answer is a Government in control of its spending, a Government with its eye on the future, a Government that is in the process of changing the direction of the Canadian economy in order that it will meet the challenges of tomorrow's world. The Budget has shown Canadians that we are meeting our commitments of four years ago and that we are prepared to meet the challenges that the future will bring.
Since 1984 the Government has revitalized the private sector and restored fiscal responsibility to government financing. This has been accomplished by reducing the deficit from $38 billion in 1984 to $29.3 billion where it stands today. This is a tremendous achievement. In 1984 many Members on the opposition benches stated that we could not do it, but it has been done. The Government and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) have done it, and we will continue along this path of slow but steady economic growth.
The deficit was only one problem that we inherited from the Liberals. Between 1980 and 1984 government spending had increased by some 14 per cent, which far exceeded the rate of inflation in the same period. Under the Liberals government spending doubled in a short period of five years.
This Government has managed to turn all of this around. In the first three years of our mandate we cut spending to 3.5 per cent, less than the rate of inflation. If we had not taken immediate action Canadians would have been faced today with an extra $100 billion more on our national debt.
The Budget-Mr. Corbett
It is because of this Government's steady hand over the past three years that we are able to announce an increase in government program spending of 4.3 per cent for the coming fiscal year. It is true that deficit reduction and economic growth will slow down in the coming year. We will continue to have growth and we will continue to trim the deficit.
The Government has been solidly committed to the strength of the Canadian economy and the future of the nation. As the Hon. Minister of Finance so aptly pointed out in his Budget Speech, Canada has done better than any other of the major industrialized nations. Canada is number one in economic growth. This is reflected in the growth of investment and in the creation of new industry and business across the country. Canada is number one in employment growth. The national average unemployment rate has fallen to 8.1 per cent in January from 11.7 per cent in September, 1984. In New Brunswick the unemployment situation that this Government inherited was considerably worse. In 1984 the unemployment rate in my home province was 16.2 per cent, which was intolerably high. Today I am pleased to report that this figure is down to 12.5 per cent. It is still too high, but there has been a real reduction of 3.7 percentage points. This is significant progress, progress that has led to the creation of 1.150 million jobs nationally since 1984 and 33,000 jobs in New Brunswick. These are good, well paying jobs, unlike those created by the quick fix band-aid program of Liberal make-work projects. Economic and employment growth were spread more evenly among the regions last year, and unemployment dropped in every province.
There is not much good news. Unfortunately, Atlantic Canadians have not been in a position to accept or absorb it all. The Opposition has stated that it is pledging to help the Atlantic region. But when it comes time to cast a vote for Atlantic prosperity in the House of Commons, suddenly the Opposition is whistling a different tune. In case my colleagues opposite have short memories, the NDP voted against the initial payment of $127 million designed for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. The NDP voted against $17 million for Atlantic Canada's fisheries.
To add insult to injury, the socialist finance critic, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy), was in Quebec not very long ago telling the shipyard workers, as my colleague from Saint John pointed out, that if the NDP were making the decisions, Montreal would have been allocated the second batch of frigates and not Saint John. I for one am glad that the NDP is not making the decisions. I can tell you, Madam Speaker, so are a lot of shipyard workers in Saint John, New Brunswick.
The NDP and that Hon. Member ought to be ashamed. The socialists think that they can pit region against region and then sop up votes from the aftermath. I can say that that will not work. New Brunswickers recognize the NDP for what it is. New Brunswickers will reject the NDP in the next election as they have done in past elections.

February 25, 1988
The Budget-Mr. Corbett
I would like to point out that my colleagues on the Liberal benches will be pleased to note that not one single person year of employment for the construction of the second batch of frigates will go to any Toronto shipbuilding yard. That is because they have been complaining bitterly and constantly about all of the jobs being allocated to Ontario. They must be pleased that not one single job of that contract will go to a Toronto shipbuilding yard.
There are many things that I want to say and deal with, but 1 see that my time is running short. I wish to close by saying that fostering and guiding economic renewal is not an easy, or, as we have seen, a popularity building achievement. Significant growth, job creation, economic stimulation, international competitiveness, and deficit reductions are simply not sexy issues. But they are issues that affect the social and fiscal fabric of every region of Canada.
This Government and the Finance Minister are to be commended for applying a fiscal strategy that is responsible and rewarding. Canadians can see the difference between policies determined by what is popular, and policies determined by what is right.

I wish to congratulate my colleague, the Hon. Member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Corbett), for an excellent address. I would like to ask for his opinion on a couple of matters.
After reaching $29.8 billion in 1984-85, financial requirements are projected to drop to less than $10 billion by 199293. Relative to GDP, financial requirements will have dropped from 6.7 per cent in 1984-85 to 1.2 per cent in 1992-93. A mess like this cannot be turned around in four years.
We have to keep reminding the Canadian people who was the architect of the debt. When the Leader of the Liberal Party, the Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Turner), became Finance Minister in 1972 there was a surplus of $700 million in the Treasury. By the time the Leader of the Opposition had finished as the Finance Minister the debt added up to $5 billion. That is what is known in Canada as the "Turner formula". Following Liberal Finance Ministers continued with the "Turner formula", and we ended up with this massive billion dollars of debt. We cannot forget to remind the people of Canada who was responsible for starting this mess in the first place.
The Hon. Member for Fundy-Royal pointed out the progress that has been made in eastern Canada and in his Province of New Brunswick. I would like to get his opinion on what he thinks of the National Energy Program and the devastation that it did to western Canada. Here is what the Liberal Party and its NDP cohorts did to western Canada. In a recent edition of the Western Report it stated, "Ex-Liberal Energy Minister Marc Lalonde admits publicly for the first
time that the purpose of the NEP was to prevent the West from growing too wealthy".
Can anyone imagine two political Parties working together to plot against the West? It was devastating. Small companies had to lay people off. At the time I read into the record all the firms in Quebec and Ontario that suffered from the National Energy Program. The Member for Bourassa (Mr. Rossi) thinks it is a big joke.

Marc Lalonde also stated, "Our proposal was to increase Ottawa's share appreciably so that the share of the producing provinces would decline significantly and the industry share would decline somewhat". Well, it declined the energy industry in the West. There were lay-offs in the West and it affected all types of firms in Quebec and Ontario. Now the Liberals and the New Democrats are opposing the free trade agreement which, when implemented, will bring untold wealth to western Canada.
I would like to ask a question of my hon. friend. The trade deal was not cooked up overnight in a kitchen. It has been studied to death. In November 1982, the then Liberal Government appointed a royal commission to study economic union and development prospects for Canada. Some three years and $24 million later the Macdonald Commission presented its report which overwhelmingly recommended that Canada pursue free trade with the United States. We cannot ignore a $24 million study.
In March 1974, the Liberal dominated Senate conducted a study in its foreign affairs committee of Canada-U.S. relations. Some eight years and over 100 witnesses later, the committee presented its report which overwhelmingly recommended that Canada pursue free trade with the United States.
How can we ignore these studies? It is incredible. Millions of dollars have been spent doing sound research, and political Parties say that it is no good. They do not know what they are talking about.
The Canadian Manufacturers' Association and many business and agricultural groups support the free trade proposal as well. I should like to ask my hon. friend to whom he thinks we should be listening. Should we be listening to the detailed studies of the Senate committee and the Macdonald Commission, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, or the NDP?

In response to my hon. colleague's questions, I will attempt to deal with them as I recall them. There is no question that one of the most substantial or significant problems with which we as Canadians are faced today and must deal is the fact that over the past number of years, particularly prior to the current administration, we have been treated to a runaway spree of deficit financing primarily by a Liberal administration. As a result, tremendous and huge debts have built up.
I remind my hon. colleague that if one looks at the Budget Papers one will see that in 1984-85 we inherited $22.3 billion worth of public debt charges. If we take that particular amount and add it constantly over the four years we have been in control of the purse-strings, we will see that it totals some $88 billion. I well remember as an easterner the devastation of the National Energy Program. 1 remind my hon. colleagues opposite that back a short time ago they voted against an extra $7 million for Enterprise Cape Breton. The Liberal Members from that region should be downright ashamed of themselves. Indeed, that is what they did.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have a chance to say a few words this afternoon on the Government's Budget Papers. As we see by looking at the document, it is very thin. It does not contain very much. It is in both official languages, so it is actually half as thin. The document does not say very much.
When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) spoke a couple of weeks ago, he did not say very much. It almost seems like an accounting document, one that he could have easily tabled in the House, because it did not contain very much to help Canadians.
Over the past three and a half years taxes have increased dramatically, to some $22 billion for average citizens, whereas during the same period of time they have increased very little, if any, for corporations. That is fitting; that is what we thought the Tories would do. It is not what they said they would do. In the election campaign three and a half years ago, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said that he would have a great, new egalitarian society. However, when we look at this document and look at what has happened over the past three and a half years, we see what the Government is planning to do. What it has been doing in each statement is trying to pull the fabric of our nation apart, making a very rich section and a very poor section. The Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) said that it really creates two Canadas, a rich Canada and a poor Canada. That is what the Government has been about in this document which really does have many new changes, although I would like to talk a little bit about the changes later on.

February 25, 1988
The Budget-Mr. Foster
Our real concern is the impact which this Budget and previous Budgets will have on Canadians. If we look at the taxes which have been imposed on Canadians since September, 1984, we find litany of regressive direct sales taxes, excise taxes, all of those taxes which hit low income people more than the high-income people. The whole tax reform is to bring down the income tax scales so that those in the high-income tax brackets will benefit and those in the low income brackets will benefit very little, if at all.
When the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance talk about taking 850,000 people off the tax rolls with a tax reform program, they fail to mention that practically one million Canadians have been put on tax rolls by tax increases imposed since 1984. Although this Budget is a very thin document, in this one year alone, 1988, the Government has imposed $2 billion worth of new taxes, most of them imposed on a regressive basis via sales tax excise taxes on gasoline and a whole host of other things.
If you glanced through the document you would say it is not bad, that only a 1 cent a litre tax on gasoline showed up. But if you look closely at the taxes applied in 1988, you will see different things coming from tax reform and from previous taxes which start January 1, 1988 and amount to $2 billion. I cannot do the calculation rapidly enough to give the exact across-the-board increase, but it is an extremely heavy load in this one year. There was the 1 cent a litre gasoline tax, which draws down $300 million. There was an additional sales tax of $300 million, which came into effect with this Budget. On top of that, on January 1 there is a 10 per cent tax on long distance phone calls amounting to $870 million.
I had a small businessman in the marina business contact me about that and he said it amounted to something like $80 or $90 in additional taxes on his small business which commenced at the start of the year when business is slow. There is a 12 per cent tax on wallpaper, which will amount to about $60 million. From the 1985 Budget there is deindexation of the income tax scales, which add another $750 million. Even though the document is very thin it rides very hard on low-income people and on senior citizens because practically every tax is a regressive excise or sales tax. There is very little lifted from the ordinary low income Canadians in this exercise.
It is interesting that in the calculation which our caucus did, the average family with an income of $32,000 a year will pay about $1,200 per year more this year than it did in 1984. This calculation is based on all of the increases which have taken place during the last three years. The tax load has been especially onerous for the average family. In northern Ontario the increase in gasoline taxes, which amount to 5 cents a litre or 23 cents a gallon since 1984, we consider to be a special tax on northern Ontario. I am sure areas in western Canada and in the north consider it a special tax placed on their regions because of the longer distances people have to travel. That 1 cent a litre tax increase generates some $300 million, and in
the Budget Papers it was set exactly beside the loss of revenues and tariffs in the Canada-U.S. trade deal.
The Prime Minister talked about a free trade deal. If you look at it you find that the tariffs which are reduced by some $400 million in the first fiscal year of the free trade deal cost some $460 million. In the first three months of 1989 it will cost some $55 million and the new taxes generated from this 1 cent a litre extra will little more than cover the loss of those tariffs.
The Government's anticipation of increased jobs over the first five years of the free trade deal are estimated at 120,000 jobs or 24,000 a year. That was calculated on the basis that the tariffs would be lifted, and over the five years it would amount to some $2 billion. In fact, if you look closely now that this gas tax has been imposed, you will find that there will be no reduction in taxation for the ordinary Canadian. In fact what Canadians would pay less in tariffs they will pay more in gasoline taxes.
Certainly over the 10 year period Canadians will pay a great deal more, perhaps $700 million or $800 million more. But there is one difference. Tariffs, whether on poultry meat or a seasonal tariff on tinned fruit and vegetables produced in the Niagara area or in the Okanagan Valley, help protect Canadian industry, Canadian agriculture and Canadian jobs, whereas the excise tax placed on gasoline is a straight dead weight.
For the sake of those who might have forgotten how much additional taxes have been imposed since 1984, we should look at all the indirect tax increases. We have had a 25 per cent increase in sales tax from 9 to 12 per cent at a cost of $3 billion extra. We had a tax for candy, soft drinks and fast foods imposed in 1985 and 1987 of $460 million. I have already mentioned the wallpaper and paint tax of $60 million which started January 1. If we look at the gasoline taxes, we see an addition of over $2 billion during the three and a half year period. There have been a rash of taxes relating to alcohol, tobacco and so on. In any event, the whole tax regime has been to grind down those in low-income groups.
One decision made last year in the tax reform package was the decision by the Minister of Finance to remove the special provision with regard to the mine depletion allowance and flow-through shares. This mechanism, which was put in place in 1984, raised some $500 million or $600 million a year for mining exploration and development in areas like northern Ontario. There will be a rally here on March 1. Municipalities from all over northern Ontario, northern Quebec and the northern parts of Canada that depend on mining exploration and development will emphasize to the Government what a tremendous disadvantage the loss of the flow-through shares and the earned depletion allowance will be for the mining industry.
If those mechanisms for carrying out exploration and development are not in place, we will not have new mines or the job opportunities that are created by those new mines. I
February 25, 1988

still hope that the Minister will change his mind and make a decision to reinstate the earned depletion allowance and the flow-through shares.
1 see that the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) is here today. I know that he would want to support me in that. In resource areas like northern Ontario and Western Arctic, we depend on mining operations to provide jobs. We in Canada have not discovered many new mines in the last 10 or 15 years. If we stop providing these incentives for investment in exploration and development, of course we will not discover any more at all.
As well, I want to look at the situation in agriculture. I have long been concerned about the situation of agriculture in Canada. We were heartened to hear the Prime Minister indicate back in December that he would put some $400 million or $500 million in additional funds into the Farm Credit Corporation. As Hon. Members know, agriculture is facing one of the most difficult and trying times in history. Of the 170,000 farmers who have economic-sized farms, farms with sales of over $20,000 a year, some 40,000 farmers are in serious financial difficulty or are totally insolvent.
We have been calling on the Government for over a year now to get serious about this problem and to take some action to put the Farm Credit Corporation on a sound financial basis. We learned last April 30 that the Farm Credit Corporation had a negative equity of $124 million. That had changed from a positive equity position of $125 million in the last two or three years. We are told that by the end of this fiscal year, 1987-88, that negative equity position will be close to $300 million.
We were flabbergasted to learn when the Estimates were tabled this week that absolutely no funds had been provided to the Farm Credit Corporation in the way of appropriations. Surely the Government ought to take seriously its responsibility to the rural parts of Canada. The agriculture industry is one of the top industries for employment. It permeates the entire country. Surely the Government should have taken some action to restore the financial viability of this Crown corporation.
At the meeting of the Agriculture Committee this morning, we spoke to the new Chairman who is charged with the responsibility of establishing a recovery program. He did not know either why there was no funding provided for the Farm Credit Corporation. There is much concern across Canada that the Government may be trying to privatize it or wind it up. We do not know. We do know that the new Chairman is saying that the corporation will be hard on farmers and will force them to pay up when they are delinquent on their accounts. This is happening at a time when many farmers have been going through the worst period in history. The only explanation that seems reasonable is that the Government is refusing to provide this funding to the Farm Credit Corporation so that the corporation will go after the farmers and make them pay
The Budget-Mr. Foster
up, even though they may have to deprive their families of benefits or even of a decent living.
Those are some of the concerns I have as I go through the Budget brought down by the Minister of Finance a couple of weeks ago. I think there is so much concern because people are very uncertain about tax reform. We have heard that the income tax scales will be reduced and that in fact there will be a slight reduction in income taxes sometime in July or August of this year, a reduction of $150 to $200 for the average taxpayer. Comparing that to extra taxation through all kinds of regressive sales taxes in the past three and a half years, it does not seem like very much. There will be a reduction of $150 to $200 with an increase of $1,200. We know that the other shoe must eventually fall.
The Government is planning to bring in a new super-deluxe national sales tax which will apply not only to traditional goods and commodities but will also supposedly apply to all kinds of services. It will apply at various stages along the production of commodities. It seems to me that if tax reform had been done on a fair, equitable and honest basis, it should have been done completely. There should have been a comprehensive program so that people would not have to wonder what will happen with that sales tax increase which will supposedly take place later this fall or in the coming year. That could provide for a double whammy. Again, a sales tax is a regressive tax, one that hits everyone on an equal basis, regardless of income and ability to pay.
The Government missed an opportunity to come completely clean with Canadians in this Budget. We know that there has been massive new taxation. We know that there is new taxation coming that will apply to all kinds of services as well as to commodities. The Minister of Finance really missed an opportunity to help the regions, to provide new funding for northern Ontario, Atlantic Canada, the West and some areas in the North. He missed a chance to reinstate flow-through shares and earned depletion allowances. As well, he missed the opportunity to provide some redress to low-income families who are suffering from a massive increase in regressive sales and excise taxes. That is why we think the Budget was a missed opportunity to help the slow-growth regions of Canada and to help low-income families.

Madam Speaker, the previous speaker brought to the attention of the House the problems with the Farm Credit Corporation. I am a farmer. The cost of land went up and up and up and the Farm Credit Corporation encouraged people to take the land on at these very high prices. February 25, 1988
Adjournment Debate
I would like to know from the Hon. Member why he supported this kind of capital gains tax which caused the problem in the first place and what his solution is to the bind the FCC finds itself in today? It seems that his way of solving the problem is irresponsibly to pour more money out. It appears that the Hon. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am glad the Hon. Member for Mackenzie (Mr. Scowen), one of the most distinguished members of the Standing Committee on Agriculture, has raised this matter of capital gains. Really the problem has been of a capital loss over the last three or four years. The net asset value of the Canadian farming industry has dropped from $116 billion to around $90 billion or $95 billion. The Government has been reluctant to put in place any mechanism to deal with this problem.
The Chairman of the FCC ticked off the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) this morning by saying in committee that one of the big problems had been that the Minister brought in this program of no foreclosure on FCC mortgages, implying that he did so without putting in place any mechanism to restructure the debt. That policy was in place for I guess 18 months or so. Now, belatedly, the Prime Minister has announced that he plans to provide some $500 million, in either loans or assistance, to the FCC over the next three years. I think everyone at the meeting of the committee this morning was saying, well, we know the Prime Minister announced that; the Chairman is criticizing the Minister for the moratorium on foreclosures; putting the two together, you would ask if the Government is going to provide this extra assistance, why did it not do it in the fall of 1985 when the Minister put the moratorium into place and provide some kind of proactive mechanism to assist the large number of farmers who are facing the loss of their farms?
We know that we now have 15,000 FCC loans in arrears. We know the debt is spiraling up. If the Government had taken some action two or three years ago similar to what it is proposing now, we might have been able to save some of those thousands of farmers who are facing the loss of their land because of low commodity prices brought on by the American Farm Bill. It is unfortunate that the mechanisms put in place by the Government were so inadequate as not to save some of those farmers.
The Hon. Member has raised a very important question, we just wish the Government had brought in mechanisms to reschedule that debt or set it aside in such a way as to save more of the young farmers. According to all estimates, given the Prime Minister's estimate of a write-off of $100 million a year for the next three years, this money represents several thousand farmers. The unfortunate part is that often they are our youngest and best farmers, our most technically advanced,
those who could have made a great contribution in the years ahead. They will probably not have that opportunity any more.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, it was heartening to hear the Hon. Member support the flow-through mechanism for funneling money into mineral exploration in those parts of Canada dependent for their economic well-being on the mineral industry. Member will be familiar with the position taken by the Hon. Madam Speaker, on May 12, 1987, I raised women's concerns regarding approval of the drug Depo-Provera for use in Canada as a contraceptive. Women have had serious questions about both the long and short-term effects of this drug, how it will be marketed and for whom it will be prescribed. When 1 questioned the Minister he suggested I should not ask questions but should rely upon him and the regulatory process to solve such matters. Advocacy on behalf of concerned women he considered to be political interference.
The information I received today from the Department of Health and Welfare leads me to say thank heaven for political
February 25, 1988

speakeroldname: Mrs. Shirley Martin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in response to a question on May 12, 1987, from the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) I wish to provide the House with information regarding the drug Depo-Provera.
Depo-Provera, an injectible hormonal drug, is a product of the Upjohn Company of Canada and has been marketed in Canada since 1961. The drug is only available with a physician's prescription. It is indicated for hormonal therapy and treatment of endometriosis-a painful condition involving the lining of the uterus-in non-pregnant women, as well as for the treatment of advanced breast and uterine cancer.
The Department of National Health and Welfare is evaluating data in a new drug submission for Depo-Provera for which new claims are being made.
The Member mentioned in her comments tonight the political interference which has taken place in order to make the Minister act. That is the furthest thing from the truth, as she should know. In fact, the Department has continued and will continue to study this drug. It is the work and results of the Department on which the Minister is making his decisions.
As indicated earlier, the drug has been available for many years for other purposes both as an oral preparation under the name Provera and as an injectible preparation where its long action characteristic has been found very useful.
The new indications which are currently under review relate to hormonal therapy and conception control. As Members of the House may know, this drug has been used for years in many countries in Europe and Asia for conception control. This is the first time the drug has been proposed by the sponsor for use in Canada as a birth control agent.
Under the requirements of the food and drug regulations, the manufacturer is required to submit evidence of the safety and effectiveness of Depo-Provera for these new indications before a notice of compliance is granted to them.
In order to hear the views of interested groups regarding fertility control, a series of meetings were held in six Canadian cities, Halifax, Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, Calgary and Vancouver, in September 1986. During these meetings, a panel appointed by the Health Protection Branch heard presentations regarding fertility control issues in general. Some individuals commented on the use of Depo-Provera for fertility control. These representations are being reviewed as part of the drug evaluation process.

February 25, 1988
Adjournment Debate
The expert advisory committee on reproductive physiology, an outside committee of medical specialists, and the Department of National Health and Welfare, are evaluating all available safety data on Depo-Provera. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has repeatedly stated that full examination of all the available evidence must take place before there is any approval of this drug for the above-mentioned new indications. At the present time, Depo-Provera is not cleared for the claim of conception control.
NATIVE PEOPLES-GENEVA RESOLUTIONS ON TREATMENT OF INDIGENOUS PEOPLES/REQUEST THAT OFFICIALS BE INSTRUCTED TO SUPPORT RESOLUTIONS

Madam Speaker, earlier this week I asked a question of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) regarding Canada's position on certain resolutions dealing with indigenous peoples and indigenous rights. These resolutions are on the agenda of the current session of the United Nations Commission on Human Rights.
I asked the question this week because my office had received some very disturbing information from Geneva, from persons who are present there, that Canada has not been encouraging and supporting the passage of these resolutions. I might say that they have already been approved by the Subcommission on the Prevention of Discrimination and the Protection of Minorities and are scheduled to go to the full commission very shortly. They call for draft international standards on the treatment of indigenous peoples, second, the establishment of a study into treaties between nation states and indigenous peoples, of which we have many in Canada, and, finally, the designation of the year 1992 as the international year of indigenous rights.
These resolutions are enormously significant to the world's aboriginal peoples. They have been working toward them for several years now and the fact that they are on the agenda of the Human Rights Commission is a sign of the importance that other UN bodies place on these resolutions. If these resolutions do not receive approval when the vote is called, which is imminent-it could be later today it could be tomorrow-then years of work by the indigenous peoples of the world will be severely set back. It could be a two year or three year delay before such resolutions could again be considered. In my view, that would be tragic, and doubly tragic if a great nation like Canada were in some way instrumental in having these resolutions defeated.
Canada has the opportunity to play a positive and very constructive world leadership role with respect to these resolutions. Here in Canada we have tried as best we can through the constitutional process to give recognition to aboriginal rights, yet undefined. We have the treaties I referred to, but their implementation and significance have not been fully appreciated by the Government of Canada, nor the people of Canada. If there was an international discussion, I
believe that the clarification coming from this international discussion could be of enormous benefit here in our country.
The information I received directly in a phone call from Geneva was that Canadian officials were actively lobbying to have these resolutions defeated. I do not have the time now to specify the tactics that they were using. However, I must report to you, Madam Speaker, that they were distressing, to say the least.
On Tuesday I asked the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) if he would meet with the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and send a strongly worded directive to the officials in Geneva to desist from this lobbying practice against these resolutions and, in fact, to get behind them and to support them.
Today I received some heartening information from Geneva. The officials met with the Cree delegates who are there and apparently they have had a change of mind. They have indicated that there has been some sort of misunderstanding and, in fact, they are now prepared to get behind these resolutions and see them approved. In fact, with respect to the one on treaties, they want to see it expanded and improved. That is very good news, and we were most heartened.
However, this afternoon when my hon. friend, the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton), put a question to the Minister of State for Indian Affairs (Mr. Valcourt), he gave an answer which seemed to suggest that the old policy of delaying and holding up these resolutions is still in effect. Thus we have a difficulty here that I would like the Parliamentary Secretary or the spokesman for the Government to clarify. Either the Cree in Geneva who met with officials this morning have been misled or the Minister of State was given the wrong information, a bad briefing, and what he conveyed to the House is not correct. He is probably not responsible for that. I am not laying blame. However, it is a contradiction and it needs to be clarified.
Let me conclude by saying that the Canadian Council of Churches has strongly supported these resolutions. It has communicated this to the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs and to the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). I conclude by quoting what the Canadian Council of Churches has said. It said:
Canada's support for this United Nation's Human Rights Commission
initiative will demonstrate to the international community and to the citizens
of Canada that your Government is indeed committed to the protection of
aboriginal rights.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Canadian position at the United Nations regarding indigenous rights is clear. The Canadian delegation, headed by Mr. Gordon Fairweather, will speak on this topic tomorrow or Monday.
Canada strongly supports the resolution endorsing the continued efforts of the Working Group on Indigenous
February 25, 1988

Populations in developing global standards in the area of indigenous rights. We recognize that the core of the agreed mandate of the Working Group is universal standard-setting.
We are also in favour of broadening and strengthening the draft resolution which calls for an examination of treaties between states and indigenous populations. As in other areas of international human rights, we believe that studies and investigations must be based on objective universal criteria. Unfortunately, the phraseology of the current draft resolution on the proposed treaty study, as presently worded, does not meet this test.
On the basis of an arbitrary criterion-the existence of a treaty-such a study would focus only on the small number of indigenous populations which have treaty relationships with their Governments. A significant portion of the native community in Canada and the vast majority of the world's indigenous populations would be excluded from this study regardless of the conditions in which they live. We are not in favour of excluding native populations, whether in Canada or abroad, just because they do not have a treaty relationship with their states. To do so would not be consistent with our commitment to human rights world-wide. In addition, such a narrow study would divert attention and resources from the main task of the working group, which is universal standardsetting.
Adjournment Debate
We have various types of arrangements with our own native populations. We have aboriginal treaty rights enshrined in our Constitution. We have under way comprehensive land claims negotiations. We believe that some of our arrangements, such as the James Bay Agreement, may be models for other countries. We do not want to exclude any of these arrangements from examination on the basis of a narrow, technical criterion. We want a broad study based on clear standards and objective universal criteria that would study all arrangements-legal, practical and de facto as well as treaties-under which indigenous people live world-wide. This is the direction currently being taken by the Canadian delegation in Geneva.
With respect to other resolutions now on the table at the commission regarding aboriginal issues, Canada has not taken a position. As Members will be aware, Canada is an observer at the commission, and we therefore believe that it is the responsibility of the 43 members of the commission to assess the merits of those texts and to act accordingly.
